title: Mouni Roy Wore 300 Hours of Gujarati Craftsmanship to Cannes — and Launched an Indo-American Film While She Was at It
excerpt: The actress attended the 79th Cannes Film Festival in a hand-embroidered Patola gown to unveil her upcoming project Bombay Stories. The moment spotlighted one of India's most endangered textile traditions on a global stage.
body:
When Mouni Roy walked into the Marché du Film at the 79th Cannes Film Festival last week, she wasn't carrying the usual Bollywood baggage — no song-and-dance promo tour, no major studio backing, no franchise hype. She was there to launch the poster and teaser of **Bombay Stories**, an Indo-American project that marks a new chapter in her career. And she did it wearing 300 hours of hand-embroidered Gujarati craftsmanship.

## The Dress That Told a Story

The fitted blue gown, designed by **Puja Shah of The Patola House**, featured geometric patterns in shades of blue, red, and mustard — the hallmark motifs of **Patola** weaving, a centuries-old textile tradition from Patan, Gujarat. A satin train added drama to the silhouette, while the embroidery work alone took artisans nearly **300 hours** to complete.

"Proud to be wearing a dress crafted by Puja Shah and all the artisans who put 300 hours into embroidering this dress," Mouni wrote on Instagram. "For those who don't know, it's Gujarati Patola work, which btw I think is stunning."

https://www.instagram.com/p/DYh1AmEDY6l/

For anyone who's walked through textile exhibitions in Ahmedabad or grown up watching their grandmother unfold a Patola saree for special occasions, seeing that craft on a Cannes red carpet hits differently. **Patola** double-ikat weaving — where both the warp and weft threads are resist-dyed before weaving — is one of the most technically demanding textile arts in the world. Authentic Patola sarees from Patan can take six months to weave and cost anywhere from ₹1 lakh to ₹6 lakh.

## Cannes as a Platform for Indian Craft

Mouni's choice wasn't just a fashion statement. In recent years, a growing number of Indian celebrities have used international red carpets to spotlight Indian textiles — from **Deepika Padukone's** Sabyasachi saris at Cannes to **Sonam Kapoor's** showcasing of Indian designers at Met Galas. But the Patola gown stands apart because it centered a **regional craft tradition** rather than a Bollywood couturier.

Gujarat's Patola weavers are a dwindling community. The craft is primarily practiced by the **Salvi family** in Patan, who guard the technique closely. By commissioning a Cannes gown in Patola work, Mouni and Puja Shah effectively gave the craft an international platform that no government scheme or trade fair could replicate.

For **NRI audiences** — particularly the large Gujarati diaspora in the US and UK — the moment was personal. Patola sarees are heirloom pieces in many families, passed down through generations. Seeing the same geometric patterns reimagined as a contemporary gown at Cannes bridges the gap between the craft traditions NRIs grew up with and the global fashion conversations they now inhabit.

## *Bombay Stories* and What's Next

The Cannes appearance coincided with the teaser launch of **Bombay Stories**, described as an Indo-American production. Details remain limited, but the project appears to position Mouni in a space between Bollywood and international cinema — a trajectory that actors like Priyanka Chopra and Ali Fazal have navigated before her.

Mouni's upcoming slate also includes **Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai**, **The Wives**, and **Ab Hoga Hisaab**. After making her name through television (*Naagin*) and her big-screen breakthrough in Brahmastra, she's clearly building toward a more curated, internationally-facing career.

## The Personal Backdrop

The Cannes outing came against the backdrop of reports about Mouni's separation from husband **Suraj Nambiar**. While she didn't address her personal life during the festival, the timing of her confident, craft-forward appearances — first in a sharp black mini dress with an oversized trench coat, then in the Patola gown — read as a deliberate statement: the work speaks.

Best friend **Disha Patani** commented "Let's go, girl" with heart emojis on Mouni's Instagram post. Mandira Bedi and singer Talwinder also showed support.

For a Cannes appearance that could have been reduced to tabloid speculation about a divorce, Mouni made sure the conversation stayed on the art — both on screen and on fabric.
